title: Python for Beginners - Learn Coding with Python in 1 Hour
summary:
This tutorial, presented by Mosh Hamedani, provides a comprehensive, beginner-friendly introduction to programming in Python. The course begins by explaining the practical applications of Python—including machine learning, artificial intelligence, web development using frameworks like Django, and task automation—and guides viewers through setting up their development environment by installing the Python 3 interpreter and the PyCharm IDE.

The tutorial progresses systematically through fundamental programming concepts. Viewers learn how to handle input and output, work with variables, and distinguish between primitive data types such as integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans. Crucial programming techniques are emphasized early on, including explicit type conversion (e.g., converting user input strings into integers or floats for calculation) and manipulating text using built-in string methods and operators.

In the latter half of the lesson, control flow and data structures are introduced. Mosh explains arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators, followed by conditional branching (`if`, `elif`, and `else` statements) utilizing Python’s signature block indentation. The video concludes with hands-on examples covering repetition structures (`while` and `for` loops), sequence generation with `range()`, and managing data collections using mutable lists and immutable tuples.

---
key_takeaways: Versatile Applications:** Python is a multi-purpose programming language ideal for machine learning/data science, web development (powering sites like YouTube, Instagram, and Spotify), and desktop automation.
Environment & Tools:** Writing Python effectively requires installing the Python 3 runtime and an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) such as PyCharm Community Edition.
Type Conversion:** User input gathered via `input()` is always returned as a string. Performing arithmetic operations on user input requires explicit type conversion using `int()` or `float()`.
Indentation-Based Control Flow:** Python uses whitespace and indentation blocks rather than curly braces to group code within conditional statements (`if`/`elif`/`else`) and loops (`while`/`for`).

Data Collections:** Python features built-in collection types including mutable lists (defined with `[]`) for ordered data that changes, and immutable tuples (defined with `()`) for data that must remain constant.

**[23:44] Arithmetic Operations & Operator Precedence**
[23:45] In this tutorial, I'm going to show you the arithmetic operators that we have in Python. These are the same arithmetic operators that we have in math. For example, we can add numbers, we can subtract them, multiply them, and so on. So let me print `10 + 3`. When we run this program, we get 13. So this is the addition operator. We also have subtraction, we have multiplication, and division. Now technically, we have two different types of division operators: we have a division with one slash, and another with two slashes. Let me show you the differences. If you use a single slash, we get a floating-point number, that is a number with a decimal point. But if you use double slashes, we get an integer, a whole number.

[24:32] We also have the modulus operator, that is indicated by a percent sign, and this returns the remainder of the division of 10 by 3, so that is 1. And finally, we have the exponent operator, that is indicated by two asterisks. So this is 10 to the power of 3. So when we run this, we get 1000.

[24:54] Now for all these operators that you saw, we have an augmented assignment operator. Let me explain what it means. So let's say we have a variable called `x`, and we set it to 10. Now we want to increment the value of `x` by 3. So we have to write code like this: `x = x + 3`. When Python executes this code, it's going to evaluate this expression; the result of this expression is `10 + 3`, which is 13. Then it will store 13 in `x`. Now there is another way to achieve the same result using less code: we can type `x += 3`. What we have on line 3 is exactly identical to what we have on line 2. So what we have here is called the augmented assignment operator. So we have this assignment operator, but we have augmented or enhanced it. Now here we can also use subtraction to decrease the value of `x` by 3, we can use multiplication, and so on. So these are the arithmetic operators in Python.

[26:02] All right, let me ask you a question. I'm going to declare a variable called `x` and set it to `10 + 3 * 2`. What do you think is the result of this expression? This is a basic math question that unfortunately a lot of people fail to answer. The answer is 16. Here's the reason: in math, we have this concept called operator precedence, and that determines the order in which these operators are applied. So multiplication and division have a higher order, so this part of the expression gets evaluated first. So 2 * 3 is 6, and then the result is added to 10. That is why the result of this expression is 16. Now in Python, operator precedence is exactly like math, but we can always change it using parentheses. For example, in this expression, if you want `10 + 3` to be evaluated first, we can wrap it in parentheses, like this. Now when we execute this code, we're going to see 26, because `10 + 3` is 13, and that multiplied by 2 is 26. Let's verify this: so print `x`, and we get 26.

**[27:14] Comparison Operators**
[27:15] So you learned about the arithmetic operators in Python. Now in Python, we have another set of operators called comparison operators. We use these operators to compare values. Let me show you. So I'm going to declare a variable called `x` and set it to an expression like this: `3 > 2`. So in this case, because 3 is greater than 2, the result of this expression is the boolean `True`. So if we print `x`, we get `True` on the terminal.

[27:53] So here is the greater than operator. We also have greater than or equal to, we have less than, we have less than or equal to, here is the equality operator which is indicated by two equal signs—do not confuse this with the assignment operator. So here we are comparing 3 and 2 for equality. So if we run our program, we see `False`, because 3 does not equal 2. So here's the equality operator, we also have the not equality operator, that is indicated by an exclamation mark followed by an equal sign.

[28:29] So let's quickly recap: here are the comparison operators we have in Python: greater than (`>`), greater than or equal to (`>=`), less than (`<`), less than or equal to (`<=`), equal (`==`), and not equal (`!=`). These operators are extremely important in real Python programs because quite often we have to compare values to evaluate certain conditions. You're going to see that soon.

**[28:53] Logical Operators**
[28:54] In Python, we have another set of operators called logical operators. We use these operators to build complex rules and conditions. Let me show you. So I'm going to declare a variable called `price` and set it to 25. Now let's print a boolean expression like this: `price > 10`. Now let's say we want to check to see if the price is between 10 and 30. This is where we use the logical `and` operator. So we type `and`, and right after that we type another boolean expression: `price < 30`. So with this `and` operator, if both these boolean expressions return `True`, the result of this entire expression will be `True`. Take a look: so in this case, we get `True` because the price is between 10 and 30 dollars.

[29:46] We also have the `or` operator. With the `or` operator, if at least one of these boolean expressions returns `True`, then the result of this entire expression will be `True`. To demonstrate this, I'm going to change `price` to 5. Let me show you how Python is going to execute this code. So first it's going to look at this boolean expression: is price greater than 10? No, it's not, so it will keep going. Then it will look at the second boolean expression: is price less than 30? It surely is, so the result of this entire expression will be `True`. Take a look: there you go.

[30:25] We also have the `not` operator, which basically inverses any value that you give it. Let me show you. So we're going to have one boolean expression: `price > 10`. The result of this expression is `False`. Now if we apply the `not` operator, this will inverse `False` to `True`. So when we run the program, we get `True`. So let's quickly recap: in Python, we have three logical operators: we have logical `and`, which returns `True` if both expressions return `True`; we have logical `or`, which returns `True` if at least one expression returns `True`; and we have `not`, which inverses any value that we give it.

**[31:09] If Statements**

[31:51] The cursor is indented, and this represents a block of code. So the code that we write over here will be executed if this condition is true; otherwise, it's not going to be executed. Let me show you. So here we're going to print "It's a hot day". And by the way, note that here I've surrounded this string with double quotes because here we have a single quote as an apostrophe. So I couldn't declare a string like this with single quotes: if I typed `'It\'s a hot day'`, look, Python gets confused because it thinks this single quote represents the end of our string, so it doesn't recognize the subsequent characters, okay? So that's why we use double quotes here, so we can have an apostrophe in our string.

[32:40] So, "It's a hot day". Now if I press Enter again, the cursor is indented, so the code that we write here will be part of our `if` block, and it will get executed if this condition is true. So here we can print a second message: "Drink plenty of water". Now to terminate this block, we press Enter and then press Shift + Tab. The cursor is no longer indented, so the code that we write here will always get executed, no matter what, whether this condition is true or not. Let me show you. So here we can print "Done". Because this code is not indented, it's not part of our `if` block, okay? So let me run the program and see what happens.

[33:23] So we see these two messages because the temperature is greater than 30. Now, if I change the temperature to 25 and run the program again, we don't see those messages; we only see "Done".

[33:38] Now let's add a second condition. So if temperature is not greater than 30, that means it's less than or equal to 30. So I'm going to add a second condition: if the temperature is between 20 and 30, I want to print "It's a nice day". So here we type `elif`, that is short for else if, and here we type a second condition: `temperature > 20`. We add a colon, press Enter, now we have a new block. So here we can print "It's a nice day". So if this condition is true, that means the temperature is greater than 20 and less than or equal to 30.
